content.title: About
content.content: Dried whole eggs are fully dehydrated eggs produced by spray‑drying or freeze‑drying processes. They retain most of the nutrients of fresh eggs and can be stored at room temperature for several years.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dried eggs are widely used in the food industry for bakery mixes, sauces, and dry meal kits.
Freeze‑drying preserves over 90 % of the protein and most of the vitamin D found in fresh eggs.
Unlike liquid egg products, dried eggs do not require refrigeration.
Reconstitution is simple: add water at a ratio of about 1 part powder to 2.5 parts water by weight.
In the USDA database, dried whole eggs are listed under product code 5589.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Dried eggs provide roughly 48 g of high‑quality protein per 100 g, making them an excellent protein source.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D remains largely intact after drying, supporting bone health and immune function.

items.title: Contains biotin and vitamin B12
items.content: These B‑vitamins are important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: With virtually no carbs, dried eggs fit well into low‑carb and ketogenic diets.

items.title: Convenient storage
items.content: Shelf‑stable at room temperature, they are ideal for travel, emergency kits, and long‑term storage.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: People with egg allergy may react to dried eggs just as they would to fresh eggs.

items.title: Added sodium
items.content: Some commercial products contain added salt; always check the label if sodium intake is a concern.

items.title: Loss of heat‑sensitive vitamins
items.content: The drying process can reduce certain heat‑sensitive vitamins, such as vitamin C.

items.title: Water quality for reconstitution
items.content: Use clean, safe water when rehydrating to avoid microbial contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rehydrate dried eggs by mixing 1 tsp (about 5 g) of powder with 12 ml of water, then use as you would fresh eggs in baking, omelets, sauces, or desserts. They can also be added to protein shakes or backpacking meal packs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored, it lasts 2–3 years. Once opened, consume within about 6 months for best quality.
